description: We're a team of 3 engineering students, specializing in Robotics, AI, mechatronics, and telecommunications.
summary:
We developed Odos, an interactive 3D navigation and decision-support interface for a hypothetical crewed science EVA on Mars. The scenario targets Deuteronilus Mensae, a mid-latitude region studied as a candidate for human exploration, where radar has detected debris-covered glaciers. The EVA’s goal is to verify whether shallow water ice is present at the foot of a butte, and to sample it.

The tool fuses topography and slope, CTX imagery, TES dust cover and THEMIS day/night thermal inertia into a terrain-mechanics cost model. A custom A* algorithm computes the lowest-energy rover route from the starting point to the closest safely accessible location near the point of interest. From this location, a second EVA is planned for an astronaut on foot, who proceeds toward the butte to collect scientific samples at a designated elevation, within a safe return radius. The route is drawn on a 3D terrain view, alongside simulated telemetry for rover energy, travel time and suit oxygen.

Unlike regional tools such as Mars Trek, Odos gives astronauts a hyperlocal and safety-first view of a specific excursion.
details:
You are standing at the base, on a flat plain in Deuteronilus Mensae, Mars, at 40° north. A butte of scientific interest lies out there, your suit’s oxygen is limited, and the rover cannot climb every slope. How far can it take you, and where must you walk? Odos answers these two questions for a specific extravehicular activity, using real NASA data.

We designed the mission scenario: a hypothetical crewed science EVA at Deuteronilus Mensae, Mars (~40°N, 22°E). We chose this mid-latitude region because NASA has studied it as a candidate for human exploration, and radar has detected debris-covered glaciers there. The EVA’s goal is to verify whether shallow water ice is present at the foot of a butte and to sample it. Ice at this site is probable but unconfirmed, so the mission is framed as a verification, not as a resource-extraction task.

We then selected the exact site for the crew’s base, looking for flat terrain with gentle slopes, and a butte of interest about 5.5 km from the base. We chose a butte rather than a crater because we found no documented ice-exposing crater at our location in the USGS dataset, and a butte gives realistic slopes that force a decision between driving and walking.

Finally, we gathered the data to support this scenario and cropped it to a 10 km × 10 km zone around the butte. We kept only datasets that were consistent with each other in resolution and coverage, and we accepted their limits. At 24 m per pixel, boulders and small obstacles are invisible, so the plan flags them as unknown hazards to be confirmed before the EVA.

Our planning module computes, for a start point and a target chosen on the map, the route that minimizes the energy spent. From it, it derives the duration, the rover’s battery consumption, and the oxygen and water consumed by the astronaut in the spacesuit. It helps compare EVA (extravehicular activity) scenarios and assess a site before sending a crew there.

All our data come from NASA’s Mars Trek tool resources: a CTX stereo DEM (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter) at 24 m per pixel for elevations, day and night THEMIS infrared mosaics at 100 m per pixel for temperatures, and the TES dust cover index for dust coverage. Slopes are computed on the DEM at loading time. They are used for three things: blocking impassable steps, computing the cost of each step, and choosing the rover’s parking point. Temperatures are converted into soil hardness, and dust adds a small rolling-resistance penalty for the rover.

Slope is the main exclusion criterion. A step is forbidden to the pedestrian beyond 20°, the limit for a human in a pressurized spacesuit, which matches EVA planning practice where traverses on slopes below 20° are retained. For the rover, we forbid steps with more than 12° of frontal slope and cells with more than 18° of local slope (a proxy for cross-slope). The rover also does not approach within 500 m of the target. These limits, and not an arbitrary choice, explain why it cannot always go all the way.

Our A* algorithm works on a 24 m grid. In “pedestrian” mode, the whole route is done on foot. In “rover” mode, the vehicle drives as far as its slope limits allow. If the target is on terrain too steep for it, it stops at the nearest accessible cell. We then backtrack along its previously planned route to the last flat terrain (smoothed slope below 8° over the entire 3 × 3 neighborhood), where the rover is parked, because it must never park in the middle of a slope. This backtracking is only used to choose the parking point: it is not counted as actual travel. A second, pedestrian A* leads the astronaut from the rover to the target. The return follows the same path with reversed steps, because climbing and descending do not have the same cost.

The cost of each A* step is directly the energy expended: metabolic energy for the pedestrian, battery energy for the rover. The chosen route is therefore the one that consumes the least on the grid, not the shortest or the fastest. This is a deliberate choice: energy is the resource that limits an EVA (oxygen, water, battery, crew fatigue). Minimizing energy preserves safety margins and favors routes on gentle slopes and firm ground, whereas a path minimizing distance or time could cross steep or loose areas. Crew safety is our design priority.

Walking cost is based on empirical biomechanical models. The Pandolf equation, from military physiology, estimates the metabolic cost of walking with a load and already serves as the basis of a NASA Johnson Space Center EVA model. The Santee correction, also from military research, handles descents. Speed follows Tobler’s function, fitted on hiking data and applied to planetary traverse modeling during an analog mission. We adapted them to Mars: 0.379 g gravity, spacesuit stiffness, a 70 kg load and a maximum speed of 1.2 m/s.

Rover cost follows a simple force balance. Rolling resistance depends on the soil (0.04 on rock, 0.25 on sand) and is added to the weight projected onto the slope to give the force at the wheels. Battery power is the avionics power plus the mechanical power divided by the motor efficiency (75%). Speed decreases with sand and slope. The avionics stay powered during the EVA and are counted in the balance.

We infer soil hardness and the risk of bogging down through a proxy: the normalized day/night temperature difference indicates thermal inertia. A large difference signals a soil that heats and cools quickly, therefore loose. The resulting hardness modulates the walking cost and the rover’s rolling resistance, and triggers a block on soils that are too loose: routes therefore avoid bogging-down risks.

The originality lies in the coupling of rover and walking with a realistic parking on flat terrain, and in a hardness derived from real thermal data. The code is modular and feeds an interface where the astronaut chooses a target. The resolutions of the data differ (24 m, 100 m, a few kilometers), the hardness is relative to the zone, and lighting can disturb the daytime image. The assumptions (sampling duration, standby power, thresholds) are configurable and documented.

The application is built around three main components.

The user interface is developed using React, TypeScript, and Vite. Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, and Lucide React provide the UI components, icons, and dark theme optimized for tablet use.

The geographic visualization relies on an optimized image for the 2D map and Three.js for 3D terrain rendering and the first-person view. All views share the same local coordinate system to ensure that markers and routes remain accurately aligned with the terrain.

The processing and computation layer is implemented in Python (Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib), with computations of a few seconds. A local FastAPI connects the interface to the EVAPlanner, an A*-based path planner. Computations run in a separate process to keep the interface responsive.

GeoTIFF files remain the authoritative scientific data sources. The browser uses preprocessed assets optimized for visualization, while the planner operates on aligned numerical data.

Features :

The 2D view allows users to explore the map, zoom in and out, pan across the terrain, toggle map layers, and select starting and destination points.

The 3D view reconstructs the terrain from the actual Digital Elevation Model (DEM), allowing users to inspect the landscape and better understand the planned route.

The Astronaut POV view provides a first-person exploration experience at astronaut height, featuring route tracking, navigation guidance, and adjustable movement speed.

The planner distinguishes between rover-based and on-foot segments, then displays distances, estimated durations, and oxygen and electrical energy requirements. These outputs remain model-based estimates: Odos is a simulation prototype with no real telemetry or safety certification.
